products.description: From Publishers Weekly Starred Review. This biography, made up almost entirely of quotes from Muhammad Ali, serves as an important and apt reminder of how daring, outspoken, witty and relevant the boxing champ was and continues to be. Editor and designer Lois tells the athlete's story chronologically, beginning with his first words, "Gee-gee," a nickname his mother called him for the rest of her life. While there are plenty of asides, insults and rallying cries, including the famous "float like a butterfly, sting like a bee," Lois also includes a number of one-two narratives, including the young boxer's reaction to a newspaper photo of lynching victim Emmet Till ("It made me sick, and it scared me") and the time Ali stayed in a U.K. hotel suite next door to Prince Charles (when Ali knocked on the door, the butler curtly remarked that they had not ordered room service). While Ali had a lot to say about boxing, courage and himself (his favorite subject), he also had plenty to say about civil rights, religion and the Vietnam War. Each quote is married with an apt image, including the landmark Esquire cover in which the champ is portrayed as Saint Sebastian, with a chest full of arrows-only this reproduction is smartly annotated with the champ's own list of his tormentors (including Lyndon Johnson and Robert McNamara). dialogue.agent:
Here's the scoop on **"Dark Rose"**:

**Price:** $15.99 | **Rating:** 4.7/5 | **Reviews:** 1

Based on the features, here's the gist: It follows Private Investigator Davis Lewis, an ex-Army sergeant and former police detective who's flat broke. He reconnects with an old flame, Tessa, and gets hired to rescue a billionaire's trophy wife named Rose from a place called "Underground City." It's described as a mystery with twists, turns, and action.

One reviewer called it a "cracking good tale" with great action, flashbacks, and "pop culture references" — gave it a full 5 stars.

That said, it only has **1 review** so far, so there's less feedback to go on compared to the **"A Triple Shot of Spenser"** ($16.00, 4.8/5 with 25 reviews) — that one's from a well-established mystery author and has a lot more people vouching for it.

Would you like more details on any of the others?

result.title: Dark Rose
result.features: Private Investigator Davis Lewis has fallen on hard times. The ex-Army sergeant and former police detective has spent his last $1.50 on a cup of coffee at The Corner Diner when, by chance, he runs into Tessa, a grade school friend and a high school sweetheart. His fortunes change soon thereafter with a big case: Rescue a billionaire’s young trophy wife, Rose, from the hellhole called Underground City.Davis is successful and reaps the monetary benefits, plus a reference to another wealthy client, who hires him to find his missing sixteen-year-old daughter.Davis’ relationship with Tessa blossoms and wedding bells are in their future – after helping Rose escape her sadistic husband.“Dark Rose” is an entertaining read with twists and turns as Davis, and Tessa, unravel the mystery surrounding a desperate woman named Rose.

top_reviews.title: The "Dark Horse" scores top marks
top_reviews.text:
Just finished Dark Rose. Cracking good tale. Knowing the author’s proclivity for twists and turns in his stories, I
was not disappointed with his engaging tale of investigator David Lewis, his long-lost (now found) girlfriend Tessa and new acquaintance, the hustler and inside-man Eddie. We are on a search for a missing wife where Lewis must enter the foreboding “Underground City” with its intriguing populace, habits and rules. The reader gets a flat-out great story, very professionally told, very clean with good action and good descriptions. Relished the flashbacks, insights and pop culture references that Lewis, this down-on-his luck decorated former soldier, shares with us. I rooted for his success and his change of fortunes. Author Marshall has outdone himself and the reader is the winner.

Thanks for the details! That sounds like an interesting plot. I'm not too worried about the number of reviews, honestly. The rating is solid and the description sounds right up my alley.

But before I decide, could you also tell me a bit more about **"Covered in Color: Christo and Jeanne-Claude's Fabrics of Freedom"** ? That biography caught my eye too. What's it about?
dialogue.agent:
Here's what I found on **"Covered in Color: Christo and Jeanne-Claude's Fabrics of Freedom"** :

**Price:** $17.88 | **Rating:** 4.8/5 | **Reviews:** 8

It's a vibrantly illustrated biography about the famous artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude, known for wrapping iconic landmarks in fabric — like Berlin's Reichstag, the Pont Neuf in Paris, and New York's Central Park *The Gates*. It follows Christo from his childhood in Soviet-controlled Bulgaria (where creativity was suppressed) to international fame, and how he and Jeanne-Claude moved to New York as undocumented immigrants, becoming equal partners in life and art.

It's received a **Kirkus starred review** calling it "a gem of a biography!" and all 8 customer reviews are **5 stars** — readers call it "beautiful," "fascinating," and "a work of art."

So here's your comparison at a glance:

| Book | Price | Rating | Genre |
|------|-------|--------|-------|
| **Dark Rose** | $15.99 | 4.7/5 | Mystery/Thriller |
| **Covered in Color** | $17.88 | 4.8/5 | Biography (Art) |

Both are excellent picks! Which one speaks more to you today?

result.title: Covered in Color: Christo and Jeanne-Claude's Fabrics of Freedom
result.features: A vibrantly illustrated biography about visionary artist Christo, encouraging creativity, perseverance, and appreciating the beauty all around us Christo (1935–2020) and Jeanne-Claude (1935–2009) are renowned for their large-scale, ambitious art installations that wrapped landmarks and swaths of land in fabric, including Berlin’s Wrapped Reichstag , Paris’s The Pont Neuf Wrapped , and concluding with New York City’s The Gates in Central Park (2005).    This lively biography chronicles Christo's humble childhood in Soviet-controlled Bulgaria—under a regime that suppressed individuality and creativity—to his international fame as a bold (and controversial) innovator in the art world. Christo discovered an early love of art and found a way to make a living out of his passion by wrapping bottles, cans, stacks of magazines, and even an air conditioner. When he met his wife, Jeanne-Claude, they moved to New York City as undocumented immigrants and became equal partners in both life and work—he, the artist, and she, the dealmaker.    Together, Christo and Jeanne-Claude made elaborate, visually stunning installations that transformed public spaces around the world, all free to the public. Christo never explained why he felt compelled to wrap things in fabric—rather, his work celebrated individual interpretation and the simple joy of seeing something familiar in a new way. And though each work was temporary, their awe-inspiring designs, uniting nature with the manmade, stayed with viewers long afterward. Covered in Color inspires readers to appreciate the beauty around us, however fleeting, and to push the boundaries of "possible."

top_reviews.text: Expansive and extravagant colored wraps around buildings, shorelines and even islands is a lifetime artistic expression of release from a childhood of Nazi restrictions and communist confines for the renowned artists in a biography bound to ignite a sense of possibility in young minds.
